body.goals: Capital growth after costs and taxes. The money is not needed at a fixed date: the horizon rolls forward, and every stock thesis must pay off within a rolling 2-3 year window. Core-satellite: a core of low-cost global equity ETFs and stable large-cap stocks, plus satellite stocks that must beat a broad global equity ETF benchmark after costs and taxes or give their weight back to the core. The stocks are run as an event- and fundamentals-driven rotation: take profits when a thesis has played out and reinvest them in the opportunity with the highest risk-adjusted expected return, switching only when the gain clears the cost of switching. Quant and risk figures (volatility, downside, correlation, contribution to portfolio risk) are part of the fundamentals of every decision. Diversified across sectors, countries and risk tiers (core, growth, speculative); every stock is justified by a written thesis built from news, fundamentals and deep research. Capital preservation still matters: avoid deep drawdowns, cut losers whose fundamentals fail, and buy theses that still hold at their buy targets when markets fall.
body.notes:
STRATEGY PRINCIPLES
1. Goal and horizon. Capital growth after costs and taxes. The money is not needed at a fixed date: the horizon rolls forward, and each stock thesis should pay off within 2-3 years from when it is written (a thesis needing longer is speculative). No glide path; if a fixed need for the money appears, then over the 12-18 months before the date move the amount needed into cash or short-term bonds, starting with the weakest theses.
2. Portfolio structure. (a) CORE: 40-60% of the portfolio, held for the long term, made of (i) one or two low-cost, broad global equity ETFs (UCITS, accumulating), which need no thesis, are not traded and are exempt from the 10% cap (until the exempt list in plan task Q8.0 exists, ignore the max-single-position alert for them), and (ii) stable stocks that meet every core-tier criterion of principle 3, each with a written thesis, the 10% cap and the normal reviews, but held long and not rotated unless the thesis breaks (principle 9). ETF holdings count toward the 10%-per-company look-through limit. There is no minimum ETF share: the core may consist of stable stocks alone. (b) SATELLITES: 10-20 individual growth and speculative stocks, at most 10% each, run as an event- and fundamentals-driven rotation (principle 6). (c) Caps: 35% per sector, 70% per country, at least 8 positions, cash 5% (max 20%); cash above 10% for more than 3 months is put to work in the best bench idea or the core ETFs. (d) Instruments: plain stocks and unleveraged ETFs only, no leveraged, inverse or derivative products. (e) Currency: no cap on foreign-currency exposure (a deliberate choice; base currency is CZK), but prefer EUR-quoted listings and ETF share classes when they are otherwise equivalent, and convert currency in batches rather than per trade to limit Trading212's FX fee.
3. Risk tiers. Every holding carries exactly one tier (dimension 'risk'); a broad index ETF is CORE. Stocks are assigned in this order. SPECULATIVE if ANY applies: market cap below USD 2 bn, OR annualised volatility above 35%, OR not yet profitable / under 3 years of profitable history. CORE only if ALL apply: market cap above USD 10 bn, AND annualised volatility at or below 25%, AND profitable for 5+ years. GROWTH is everything else. Reclassify at the thesis review date or when a criterion changes. Tier limits: core at least 40% of the portfolio, growth at most 45%, speculative at most 10%. A speculative stock may only be bought with a cash runway of at least 2 years (cash over the trailing operating cash burn, for an unprofitable company) and share dilution of at most 10% a year; open-market buying by insiders strengthens the case.
4. Risk limits (strategy `risk`). A breach forces a thesis review; on its own it is never a sale. (a) Portfolio volatility at most 20% a year. (b) A position down 25% or more from cost needs a thesis review; with a fundamental miss, principle 9d applies. (c) No single company above 10% counting ETF holdings. (d) No two holdings with return correlation above 0.85 that together weigh 10% or more. (e) Each stock's contribution to portfolio volatility at most 8% of the total (its risk budget). (f) A position above the 10% cap is judged on its outlook, not its size: while the thesis and deep research still project growth (KPIs on track, valuation leaves upside), hold it, add nothing and let deposits and other positions dilute it, re-checking at each review; once the projected growth is exhausted or the thesis is weakened, trim it back to 8%. Backstop (proposed, edit if unwanted): above 15% it is trimmed to 10% regardless of outlook. (g) Portfolio drawdown from its 1-year peak at most 20%. When it is hit, review every thesis within 2 weeks and freeze new speculative buys; the core ETFs, and core and growth stocks whose thesis is re-confirmed, may still be bought at their buy targets (a drawdown is when buy targets are reached). Speculative buying resumes once the drawdown is back under the limit.
5. The thesis. No stock is bought without one, built from recent news, fundamentals and deep research. It states: (a) why it is owned, its KPIs and its exit conditions; (b) the valuation: bear, base and bull values per share from intrinsic value (earnings or free cash flow per share a few years ahead) with their probabilities, the valuation method and date, and the sell and buy targets (the thesis's price target fields, checked after each sync); (c) the expected return: the probability-weighted value against the current price, annualized to the catalyst date (30% within a year beats 40% over three); (d) the risk profile: the bear-case loss, checked against the stock's historical maximum drawdown and Expected Shortfall; the expected volatility band; and the stock's correlation with the portfolio and its marginal contribution to portfolio risk; (e) the story test: the growth rate the current price implies (reverse DCF) checked against base rates (how often companies of that size and sector have achieved it); a pre-mortem (the three likeliest reasons the stock loses 40%, each made an exit condition); and the variant perception (what the owner believes that the market does not, and what evidence would prove it wrong; a thesis with no difference from consensus fails the return hurdle); (f) the conviction (1-5) and the main reason for owning it (quality, value, catalyst, momentum or other).
6. The decision loop. Trades are driven by fundamentals, events and risk: profits are taken when a thesis has played out and the money is rotated into the opportunity with the highest risk-adjusted expected return. Price matters only through the expected return it implies (a rise lowers it; a fall raises it while the value holds) and through a large loss with a fundamental miss (principle 9d). A price fall alone is never a reason to sell. The loop runs at every review and after every result, guidance change or event for a holding or bench idea: (1) update the expected return and risk profile (principle 5); (2) sell a broken thesis or a principle 9d loser, and review a stock whose risk profile left its band (principle 9c); (3) rank holdings and bench ideas (principle 7c); (4) rotate where the switching rule says so (principle 9f); (5) size within the caps and risk budgets (principle 8b); (6) put proceeds and deposits into the best bench idea, else the core ETFs (principle 8c); (7) once a year, score the decisions and switches (principle 11b).
7. Finding and ranking ideas. (a) First filter: a stock goes to deep research only if it is in the top third of its universe and sector on a combined quality, value and momentum score (quality: gross profit to assets, ROIC, stable margins, low leverage; value: free-cash-flow yield and EV/EBIT against peers and the company's own history; momentum: the 12-month return excluding the latest month) and shows no red flag (total assets growing over 25% a year without matching profit growth, share dilution over 10% a year, accruals well above operating cash flow, listed for under 2 years, or an unprofitable, small, highly volatile story stock). Quality and value carry most of the weight; strongly negative momentum means waiting for the thesis's catalyst rather than skipping the idea. An idea outside the filter needs a written reason in its thesis. (b) Events with measured edge raise a candidate's priority: an earnings surprise followed by rising estimates, a raised guidance, insider cluster buying (two or more insiders buying on the open market within 90 days), a spin-off, and a large buyback at a low valuation. Headlines alone are not an edge: the news pipeline serves mainly to catch broken theses fast. (c) Ranking: holdings and bench ideas are ranked by (annualized expected return minus the cash rate) divided by their marginal risk to the portfolio, using standalone volatility until the covariance model exists. A stock improves the portfolio when its risk-adjusted return exceeds the portfolio's times its correlation with the portfolio, so a diversifying idea can outrank a more correlated one with a higher expected return; an idea that adds to the portfolio's dominant factor bet needs a higher expected return to compensate. Under-represented sectors, countries or tiers only break ties between comparable ideas; never take a weaker idea just because it fills a gap. (d) The bench: keep 5-10 researched candidates, each with a full thesis and buy target, so profits are redeployed at once into a prepared idea rather than a rushed one.
8. Buying and sizing. (a) A stock is bought or added to only when its thesis is intact (re-confirmed at its last review, no open principle 9b trigger), its expected return is at least 30% over the thesis horizon (about 10% a year above the market's expected return), its base-case upside is at least twice its bear-case loss, and it ranks at the top (principle 7c). Its buy target is the price at which it first passes these, so reaching it is a prompt to act. The core ETFs have no hurdle. (b) Size: a new stock starts at no more than 5% (core), 3% (growth) or 1.5% (speculative) and within its risk budget (principle 4e), proportional to its risk-adjusted expected return and reduced for higher volatility (roughly expected return divided by variance, used as a ceiling, never a target); it may then grow within the caps and the risk budget. Ahead of a binary event (a trial result, a regulatory decision, an earnings report with large historical moves), hold a smaller position and add after the event. (c) Deposits and sale proceeds go first to the core (the core ETFs, or a core-tier stock that passes principle 8a) while the core is below 40%, then to the most under-represented risk tier, sector or country, and within it to the highest-ranked holding or bench idea above the return hurdle; when none is ready within 3 months, to the core ETFs. Never into a position already above its cap.
9. Reviews and selling. (a) Cadence: core and growth every 3 months, speculative monthly, and after every quarterly report and every trigger below. Every review ends with a written decision (hold, add, trim or sell), refreshed scenarios, expected return, risk profile and targets, and the reason; a hold without refreshed figures is not a completed review. (b) Triggers that force a review (never an automatic sale): the thesis requirements are no longer met (a quarterly report misses the thesis KPIs or expectations); a guidance cut or profit warning; M&A involving the company; a dividend cut or suspension; regulatory or legal action (escalated when it bears on the thesis); any other severity-3 news event; a passed review date. A broken thesis (an exit condition or a trigger confirmed by the review) is sold at once. (c) Risk triggers: a risk-limit breach (principle 4), or realized volatility above 1.5 times the thesis band over 3 months (something may have changed in the business, its leverage or its competition), forces a review, never an automatic trade; each review also checks the bear case against what the stock has actually done. (d) Losers: a stock down 25% or more from cost that also has a fundamental miss (a thesis KPI breach, or a guidance cut or profit warning) is sold, unless a written re-underwriting within 2 weeks sets a new sell target at least 30% above the current price on the same valuation method. (e) Taking profit: when a stock reaches its sell target, re-run the research and update the thesis and its scenarios within 2 weeks. Targets rest on intrinsic value, so they rise when the business keeps growing and stay put when only the price has caught up; a target may only be raised on improved fundamentals (higher earnings estimates, KPIs beating the thesis, a better outlook), never because the price rose, and the review records what changed. If the new thesis still gives a holding-worthy expected return, hold; if not, take the profit by the switching rule. (f) Switching rule: rotate from a holding to a better idea only when the gap in expected return over the thesis horizon exceeds the switching hurdle (the tax on the exact lots sold, plus trading and FX costs, plus a safety margin of 5 percentage points) and the switch improves the portfolio's risk-adjusted expected return with the risk limits, tier caps and risk budgets held after the trade. Sell the whole position when the gap is large, part of it when the gap only just clears the hurdle, and reinvest in that idea at risk-equivalent size: a more volatile replacement gets proportionally less (an 8% position at 28% volatility becomes about 5% at 45%), and the rest goes to the next bench idea or the core ETFs.
10. Costs, taxes and turnover. (a) Hold a new position at least 3 months unless its thesis breaks or it reaches its sell target; keep yearly turnover (sales over the average portfolio value) under 100%; weigh fees, FX conversion costs and tax in every trade decision. (b) Tax (assumes Czech tax residency; verify with a tax adviser): gains on shares held more than 3 years are tax-exempt (the time test, counted per purchase lot), and sales whose total gross proceeds stay under CZK 100,000 a year are exempt. So: from 30 months of holding a lot, a reached sell target leads to a trim or a hold rather than a full sale until the lot passes 3 years, unless the thesis is broken, and a switch is compared with switching after the time test; plan trims to use the CZK 100,000 annual exemption; compare every sale's after-tax result with holding to the time test; when selling part of a position, sell the lots older than 3 years or at a loss first, as far as the broker's lot accounting allows; realize losses on broken theses in the same calendar year as large taxable gains, so they offset them. (c) Currency: the monthly review splits each position's CZK return into the stock's own return and the currency effect.
11. Learning. (a) The satellites must earn their place: the monthly review compares the satellite stocks' return with a broad global equity ETF benchmark (a core ETF if one is held, else the benchmark the owner names) over a rolling 2 years, after costs and taxes. If the satellites trail by more than 2 percentage points a year, move 10 percentage points of the portfolio from satellites to the core at the next rebalance (selling the stocks with the weakest theses first, within the tax rules of principle 10b), and repeat each year until they no longer trail. (b) Once a year, a decision scorecard reviews the process: the share of sell targets hit and how long they took, returns by conviction level and by main reason, the stocks bought compared with the ideas researched but rejected, every switch (the stock bought compared with the stock sold, from the switch date), and whether the risk estimates held (realized volatility and losses against the stated band and bear case). If switches do not beat holding, raise the switching safety margin (principle 9f); the weight given to each kind of idea follows what the scorecard shows works.

rules.description: No single stock above 10% of the portfolio; the core ETFs are exempt (ignore this alert for them until plan task Q8.0 adds an exempt list).
